source.title: An Empirical Study of Scaling Law for OCR
source.authors: Rang Miao; Zhenni Bi; Chuanjian Liu; Yun-He Wang; Kai Han

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equation and table formatting is flattened, making the compute-law equation and some supplementary table captions less clear.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in OCR, an image-based recognition setting, rather than language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own model-size, training-data-volume, and compute scaling results for OCR. It measures word accuracy or word error rate on OCR benchmarks, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. It does not test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or downstream language-task performance. Scaling observations cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own model-size, data-volume and training-time sweeps for transformer scene-text recognition (OCR), an image-to-text setting. It fits power laws to average word error rate, so its results bear on V5 (the power-law form outside text pretraining). It measures OCR word accuracy or error, not language-model loss, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that OCR performance shows smooth power laws with model size and data volume, with compute also fitted by a power law. They add that larger models use samples more efficiently, that data-source proportions matter, and that OCR-related pretraining helps. They also note data scaling is cheaper than model scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Uses OCR model-size/data/compute sweeps and benchmark word accuracy or word error rate, rather than language-model pretraining loss. The paper describes fitting a line in log space and checking the final point against a threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that data-source proportions affect accuracy; Table 7 also changes the composition of datasets along with volume. Training hyperparameters and architecture are discussed, but the reported size sweeps do not isolate all such choices.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed ViT-S encoder, increasing PARSeq decoder depth from 1 to 5 lowers word accuracy from 95.56 to 93.77 (Supp. Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In OCR encoder-decoder transformers, decoder depth materially changes accuracy (architecture shape matters).

fits_no_version.finding: Larger PARSeq models reach lower error at an equal number of images seen and converge in fewer epochs (32/14/5 for S/B/L) (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger OCR models are more sample-efficient, mirroring Kaplan et al.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic:real data ratio has an optimum at 1:3 (96.85), and accuracy drops to 95.70 at 1:5 (Table 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data mixture, not just volume, governs OCR scaling gains.

record.problems: The measured outcome is OCR benchmark word accuracy/error, not cross-entropy loss. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The compute curve is presented graphically and its extracted equation formatting is unclear. The data-expansion experiment in Table 7 changes data composition as well as sample count.
record.rows_left_out: Individual benchmark-specific accuracies reported alongside the aggregate averages in Tables 4-7 are not separately rowed; aggregate averages are retained for each scaling condition. The supplementary Union14M tables also contain benchmark results beyond the size-sweep averages recorded here.

untested.parts: Other modalities (video, generic image models), repeated-data regimes, and fine-tuning/transfer scaling laws are not tested. The outcome is word error rate, not cross-entropy loss. Compute scaling is only shown graphically, with inconsistent equations.
Language-model held-out pretraining loss is not measured.
Language-model extrapolation is not tested. The only holdout is one OCR point about 2x beyond the fit.
No compute-optimal parameter/data allocation is fitted.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count for language-model loss.
Downstream prediction from pretraining loss is not tested.
Fitting choices and setups are not compared.

missing.what: Figure 4: average word error rate versus images seen for PARSeq-S/B/L. Larger models reach lower error at equal samples seen.
The compute-law exponent conflicts between text (-0.3271) and figure (-0.764); no compute values are tabulated.

record.verdict_notes: Measure is word error rate on 6 STR benchmarks, not loss. TrOCR sizes differ in pretrained initialisation and in batch size/learning rate, so the size sweep is confounded. The fit check uses one held-out point with a deviation threshold of 0.1. Section G claims a document-domain power-law validation, but Table 8 compares only CLIP4STR-L trained on two datasets, not a size sweep. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolating language-model loss from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how both quantities scale with compute.
Whether architecture details change loss only slightly at fixed parameter count.
Tests OCR recognition, but not other modalities such as video, or scaling laws for repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer. The outcome measure is OCR accuracy/error rather than cross-entropy loss.
Does not test downstream language-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or language-model scale.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups to establish how exponents or optimal allocations depend on them.

relationships.condition: TrOCR model-size sweep (43M–1B params, MJ+ST data)
relationships.reason: Error falls roughly linearly in log-log with exponent 0.223; the held-out TrOCR-H point lies on the fit from S/B/L (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Error followed an approximate power law with exponent 0.223, and the held-out TrOCR-H result lay on the smaller-model fit.

relationships.condition: PARSeq on REBU-Syn and PARSeq/CLIP4STR on Union14M, high-accuracy regime
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises only 0.1–0.9 points over 6–30x parameters. Fitted exponents are 0.018, -0.036 and -0.013, near flat, so the size law is very weak near ceiling (r5–r8, r21–r26).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased only 0.1–0.9 points across 6–30× parameter increases, with near-flat fitted exponents of 0.018, −0.036 and −0.013.

relationships.reason: Error falls overall (49.65%→6.91%), but in steps. Doubling data gives about 2 points twice and 12–22 points at other steps, and the 75M point changes data source. A smooth single power law is not cleanly shown (r10–r14).
relationships.display_finding: Error decreased from 49.65% to 6.91% in uneven steps: doubling data yielded approximately 2 points twice and 12–22 points elsewhere, while the 75M endpoint changed data source.

relationships.condition: PARSeq-S data expansion by adding datasets
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises monotonically (95.57→96.85), but volume and composition change together. Authors stress data-source proportion matters and no fit is given (r17–r19).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 95.57 to 96.85 as data volume and composition changed together, with source proportions emphasized and no fitted scaling law.
